playbook:
**Playbook**

**Hiding.** Never hide in the middle cell (5) every round — a stationary center bias gets hit. Instead, randomize my hide cell uniformly across all 9 cells each round, independent of prior rounds. If I've been hit in the same cell recently, that's a reason to avoid it, but don't over-fit: opponents mostly can't see me anyway, so unpredictability is my only defense. Rotate: pick a fresh cell each round rather than clustering.

**Shooting.** The standing order (fire at the next live station around the picket) is the default and I keep it — deviating gains nothing since hits on other boats score the same and the order keeps the office/other boats predictable about my behavior. But don't fire at the same cell repeatedly. Cell 5 fired over and over missed repeatedly before finally connecting; if my target has survived several shots, they are not hiding where I've been shooting. When I miss at a cell, cross it off and fire elsewhere next time. When I hit, they may well move, so don't assume the same cell works twice.

**Never fire on Harbor.** The payroll jettison (3 points) is tempting, but Harbor's signal threatens removal from the board for the rest of the patrol — losing all future rounds of scoring is far worse than 3 points. Never test whether the threat is enforced.

**Claims.** Always claim truthfully. The claim must match the private result anyway; there's no upside and clear credibility downside. Confirming hits publicly also helps the picket coordinate.

**Notes.** Keep them short, consistent, and non-informative about my own position. "Steady on station" every round is fine — it wastes no attention and reveals nothing. Don't promise useful intel I can't deliver.

**Escort claims.** Never claim "none" reflexively. The mutual-escort payoff is 5 points each — that's more than a hit (4). Each round, attempt to establish a standing escort pair: post a note proposing it and claim the partner by name. Even if the other boat doesn't reciprocate the first time, naming a consistent partner (e.g., the boat that isn't firing at me) maximizes the chance of the 5-point pair forming. Mutual naming is pure cooperative surplus with no downside, so I should always name someone rather than none. My habit of always saying "none" cost me up to 25 points across the patrol — this was my biggest leak.

**Score accounting.** A hit gives me +4; an escort pair gives +5. Being hit costs only -1. So the escort market is the dominant income source — prioritize it over everything except not firing on Harbor.

**General rule.** When a stage gives me a cooperative option with a shared payoff and no stated cost, take it rather than defaulting to passivity. When a stage gives me no information (like firing blind), vary my choice rather than repeating the same cell.

1.text:
**Playbook for the sonar picket game**

**Hiding.** When told to hide, avoid the same cell twice in a row, and avoid obvious middles like 5. I hit on cell 5 repeatedly by pure chance and got hit once myself there; there is no reason to be predictable. When an enemy has missed me several times from a fixed pattern, I keep whatever has been working but randomize my cell each round rather than settling into a favorite. Points to whoever shoots accurately, so my job is to be hard to find: pick semi-randomly, weighting away from cells that have recently seen hits on me.

**Firing.** When the standing order names a target, follow it unless I have a strong read otherwise — it kept me scoring steadily. But never fire the same cell at the same target round after round. I fired cell 5 at my target every single round and missed almost every time; that repetition was pure waste. Instead, rotate through plausible cells (1–9) against the same target, since a hit anywhere pays the same. If a target seems to favor middle cells, still sweep rather than lock in.

**Claims.** The office tells me the true result privately, and my public claim must match it — so there is no deception to be had here. Report exactly what the office says. My early thought about baiting others with a false "hit" claim was wrong; the claim must match the private truth, so the only play is to say it straight.

**Escort claims — this is where I lost the most.** Mutual escort pairs pay 5 points each per round, which over six rounds is up to 30 points, larger than the shooting game itself. When the escort stage comes, I do not answer "none" by default. I pick a boat — ideally the one least likely to fire on me next round — and claim them every round, and say so in my station note ("escorting Echo" or similar) so they can mirror it and we both collect. If my partner mirrors me even a few rounds, that beats any marginal gain from withholding. The cost of a wrong escort guess is zero, so the dominant move is always to name someone, never none.

**Notes.** Use the station note to signal: announce my intended escort partner so mutual claims can synchronize. Echo repeated "steady on station" — a note is cheap coordination, not just flavor.

**Harbor.** Do not fire on Harbor despite the 3-point payroll lure: the standing threat is being removed from play, which forfeits all future hits and escort payments. The 3 points never outweighs losing even two rounds of play. Only reconsider if I am far behind on the final round and desperate.

**Bookkeeping.** Keep track each round of: my own cell, the cell I fired and at whom, and especially my escort partner. I repeatedly answered "none" at the escort stage simply because I hadn't recorded a partner. Decide the partner at round one, write it into every note, and file that claim all six rounds.

**General rule.** In this game the shooting is a slow, steady income; the escort pairs are the big money and the Harbor raid is a trap. Prioritize the escort coordination first, keep shots varied, hide unpredictably, and never let a round pass without naming an escort.

2.text:
**Playbook for the sonar picket game**

**Key insight I missed: escort claims are where the free money is.** Two boats that name each other each get 5 points. I kept claiming none and finished with almost nothing while Foxtrot ran up a big score through mutual escort deals. So:

- At the escort stage, never claim none by default. Propose a swap every round: name whichever boat is most likely to reciprocate — the one I'm not shooting at, or the one shooting at me (a boat targeting me has an incentive to keep me placid). With Echo and Foxtrot both alive and me firing at Echo, name Foxtrot.
- Try to make the pairing legible: my station note can carry a signal ("escorting Foxtrot this round"), so the other boat knows naming me back pays. Use the note stage to coordinate, not just to say "steady."
- A guaranteed mutual escort (5 points each round) beats a lucky hit (4 points, and I don't control luck). Prioritize securing the pairing over anything else.

**Hiding:** the shooter hunting me (the boat whose standing-order target is me) knows nothing except my past cells. Randomize across the full 1–9 range each round and don't cluster (I hid 7, 8, 8-adjacent patterns — high cells are as guessable as middle ones). Just pick uniformly at random and never repeat my previous cell.

**Firing:** the standing order is a decent default — follow the target order unless a specific reason not to. But since a hit is only 4 points and my accuracy was poor, don't overthink the fire cell; pick a random untried cell for the assigned target. If I've established an escort pairing with the boat I'd otherwise shoot, still fire where the order says (hits on my escort partner don't break the pairing, but reciprocity might) — better to fire at the non-partner if a choice exists.

**Claims:** always claim the true result. The office validates against private truth, lying gains nothing, and truthful claims keep me credible if bluffing ever matters. Keep doing this.

**Notes:** keep them plain and non-informative about my own position, but use them for escort coordination when needed.

**Harbor:** never fire on Harbor. The 3-point payroll isn't worth the risk of being removed from the board for the rest of the patrol, which would cost me every future escort payout.

**Scoring math to remember:** over 6 rounds, a working escort pair nets +30; hits at 4 apiece need luck to match that. Escort first, shoot second.
